label: Lower Envelopes
notes: Chapter seven runs from printed page 165 to 194 and asks a single sharp question: how complicated can the pointwise minimum of n functions be? We answer it through Davenport-Schinzel sequences, whose near-linear length bound governs the combinatorial complexity of lower envelopes and the algorithms built on them.

label: What Is a Lower Envelope
notes: Given n continuous functions on the line, their lower envelope is the function returning the smallest value at each abscissa. Geometrically it is a thick boundary that hugs whichever curve currently sits lowest, and its complexity is the number of maximal arcs where one fixed function wins.

label: Segments and a First Bound
notes: For n line segments any two cross at most once, yet the envelope can still break into many arcs because segments start and stop. We want the worst-case number of breakpoints as a function of n, and naive counting suggesting a quadratic answer turns out to be far too pessimistic.

label: Davenport-Schinzel Sequences
notes: Encode the envelope by writing down which function is lowest as x increases, producing a sequence over an n-letter alphabet. No two equal letters sit adjacent, and crucially no alternation of length s plus two appears. These constraints define a Davenport-Schinzel sequence of order s.

label: The Forbidden Alternation
notes: The defining ban is on a subsequence a b a b a of the prescribed length. Two functions of bounded degree cross only a few times, so the lowest role cannot ping-pong between them too often. This is exactly the combinatorial fingerprint that two curves intersect at most s times.

label: Order Captures Crossings
notes: The order parameter s equals the maximum number of times two of the underlying functions can swap who is lower. Line segments give order three, parabolas order four, and degree-d polynomials order d. Translating geometry into a forbidden pattern is the whole engine of the chapter.

label: The Length Bound
notes: Let lambda_s of n be the maximum length of a Davenport-Schinzel sequence of order s on n symbols. The headline result is that lambda_s of n is almost linear: linear for small orders and only barely superlinear in general, with the inverse Ackermann function controlling the gap.

label: Why Near-Linear
notes: Order one and two sequences have length at most n and 2n minus one. Order three already needs the inverse Ackermann function, giving length n times alpha of n. The slow growth means envelopes are essentially as simple as a single function up to a near-constant factor.

label: Envelope Complexity Theorem
notes: The bridge theorem states the complexity of the lower envelope of n curves pairwise crossing at most s times is exactly lambda of s comma n. Combinatorics and geometry coincide: counting forbidden patterns counts envelope arcs, so the near-linear bound transfers directly to the picture on the line.

label: Computing the Envelope
notes: A divide and conquer scheme splits the functions into two halves, recursively computes each envelope, then merges the two by sweeping left to right and taking the lower piece. The merge cost is proportional to the combined envelope length, so the total running time is near-linear times a logarithm.

label: Applications
notes: Lower envelopes solve translational motion planning by tracking the nearest obstacle along a path, support nearest-neighbor and visibility computations, and bound the complexity of a single cell in an arrangement of curves. The same Davenport-Schinzel machinery reappears whenever a pointwise extremum of many functions must be maintained.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We turned envelope complexity into a forbidden-pattern count, proved the near-linear lambda_s of n bound, and connected it to fast algorithms and motion planning. Higher dimensional envelopes of surfaces extend the story, where the analogous bounds grow harder but the Davenport-Schinzel philosophy still guides the way.
